title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Commercial and office cleaning
audience: Solo operators and team owners of commercial and office cleaning businesses who want more work from offices and commercial sites that suit their service, their area and their crew's night shifts.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, visit pattern and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a commercial cleaning need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. For commercial cleaning, write down the building types you clean well, such as offices and retail sites your crew can clean at night, the price range you can sustain (the vendor per-visit ranges help you check it), the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A three-evenings-a-week contract on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the buying decision, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Facilities managers, property managers, office landlords and tenants with several sites are examples of prospects, but add one only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Write one short profile for each segment, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market (24 September 2024), and test your assumptions against Victorian guidance on who buys (business.vic.gov.au, undated). Keep only business contact details published for business use, and keep the list secure. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (Spam Act obligations page, last updated 28 March 2019, an older source). Whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business depends on its turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's small business guidance. Its coverage is not confirmed in the research file.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a commercial need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. For commercial cleaning, these include a public notice of planned building works, a new fit-out on a street where you already work, a change of tenant at a site you already visit, or a lease that is ending. Clean Group says direct outreach to businesses with expiring contracts can work (updated 15 March 2026, a vendor guide). Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Public registers are useful signals about businesses and public bodies. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy (last updated 7 August 2026). Federally, AusTender lists open tenders and publishes awarded contracts of $10,000 or more (Department of Finance, undated). Other states and territories run their own tender systems (business.gov.au, 19 August 2025). Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register, so check your own council's register (DataVic, last updated 5 November 2026). The Commonwealth Cleaning Services Guidelines were revoked from 1 July 2014, so do not use them as current tender rules (PM&C, 2014). No office cleaning tender notice with a published price was found in the research, so check AusTender and council portals yourself.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: Before you make an offer, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline (Business Queensland, last updated 16 November 2022). A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the business or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a notice about works at its building. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined floor or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. ACMA says marketing messages need consent, and that consent should be recorded. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading. About 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). A specific message that names you is therefore an advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A pattern to test is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. The research does not source this interval, so treat it as a starting point. For a formal tender, follow the tender's own contact rules rather than your schedule. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. Every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA). At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the job, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the commercial work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message and do-not-call rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A small commercial cleaner covers three suburbs. A public notice goes up about planned repairs to the common areas of an office building in one of them, and the facilities manager's business email address is published on the building's contact page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the facilities manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (last updated 28 March 2019), and the research file warns not to assume a business-to-business exemption. So the owner first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive messages or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the manager has agreed to. For a phone call, the owner checks the Do Not Call Register guide. The research file says business numbers cannot be registered, but the guide does not settle whether calling-hour limits apply to them, so treat the limits as applying until checked: weekdays 9 am to 8 pm, Saturdays 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays. Any message that does go out names the notice, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific item it could handle, and asks one question. The owner does not contact individual tenants or staff using private details, and does not enter the common area without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, visit pattern and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact, such as a staff member's personal number.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance the state where the work is done requires before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. Marketing messages need consent, which should be recorded, and every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam'). Phone calls to business numbers face the calling-hour limits described in the do-not-call guide (2018 copyright notice). The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Its coverage of small business is not confirmed in the research file. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the commercial work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals and tender registers, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at an office building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each tenant using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. The page as read does not name the Spam Act 2003 and does not cover privacy law. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).
